title: Counting Bits
directAnswer: Return an array where ans[i] is the number of set bits in i, for all i from 0 to n. The naive answer popcounts each number independently in O(n log n). The optimal answer reuses earlier results: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), giving O(n) time and O(1) extra work per number.

remember.formula:
dp[0] = 0
for i in 1..n:
    dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
return dp
rules: `i >> 1` drops the lowest bit — it's `i` with its last digit chopped off, a smaller index already solved.
`i & 1` is the bit you chopped: 1 if `i` is odd, 0 if even.
So `bits(i) = bits(i / 2) + (last bit)` — one O(1) recurrence reuses every earlier answer.
Alternative recurrence: `dp[i] = dp[i & (i - 1)] + 1` (Kernighan: clear lowest set bit, add 1).
The output array of size n + 1 is the *answer*, not auxiliary space — extra space is O(1).
whenToUse: You need popcount for a whole range 0..n, not a single number
A bigger number's bit count can be built from a smaller, already-computed one
The interviewer asks you to beat the obvious 'call popcount n times'
Any problem where dropping/clearing one bit yields a solved subproblem
antiSignals: You only need the count for one number → Brian Kernighan, no array (Number of 1 Bits)
You need the actual bits, not the count → shift-and-mask each position
n is tiny → the O(n log n) per-number popcount is fine and simpler to write
Memory is the constraint and you can't even store the output → reconsider the problem
remember.takeaway: Counting Bits is the gateway 'bit DP' problem: the count for i is the count for a smaller number (i >> 1) plus one cheap correction. The pattern — solve a number by reusing a structurally-smaller one — is the same instinct behind every overlapping-subproblem DP.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can spot the overlapping subproblem hiding in the binary representation — that bits(i) relates to bits(i/2) — and turn an O(n log n) popcount loop into an O(n) DP.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Stopping at the per-number popcount (correct but O(n log n)), or deriving a recurrence but mis-handling the base case dp[0] = 0 or the odd-bit correction.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence from the binary structure out loud (right-shift removes the lowest bit; i & 1 restores it), mention the alternative dp[i & (i-1)] + 1, and state extra space is O(1) since the array is the required output.

problemStatement:
Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` such that for each `i` (`0 ≤ i ≤ n`), `ans[i]` is the **number of 1's** in the binary representation of `i`.

Follow-up: it is very easy to come up with a solution with `O(n log n)` time. Can you do it in **linear time** `O(n)` and possibly in a **single pass**? Can you do it without any built-in function like `__builtin_popcount`?
constraints: Follow-up target: O(n) time, no popcount builtins
understanding: Produce the set-bit count for every integer from 0 up to n, all at once. The interesting part is the follow-up: instead of counting each number from scratch, build each answer from a smaller one you've already computed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the output include index 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the array has length n + 1, covering 0..n inclusive, and ans[0] = 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is n guaranteed non-negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, so I don't need to worry about negative indices or the sign bit.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the output array count against my space complexity?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's the required output, so it doesn't count as extra space. The DP uses only O(1) auxiliary space beyond the array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use a language builtin like Integer.bitCount in a loop?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: That gives the O(n log n)... actually O(n) with hardware popcount, but the follow-up wants me to show the DP recurrence, so I'll implement it manually.

approaches.name: Per-Number Popcount (Brian Kernighan)
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this: 'I can count each number's bits independently — here's the O(n log n) version' — then improve it.
hints: You already know how to count the set bits of one number. What if you just do that for every i from 0 to n?
For each i, run Brian Kernighan's n & (n - 1) loop to count its bits and store the result at ans[i].
Each number costs O(number of set bits) ≤ O(log i), and there are n numbers → O(n log n) overall.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n + 1 numbers we run a popcount loop that costs up to O(log i) (number of set bits). Summed across the range that's O(n log n) time; only the output array, no extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Solve every index independently: for each `i` from `0` to `n`, count its set bits with Brian Kernighan's `i & (i - 1)` loop and store that in `ans[i]`.

**Why this is the honest starting point.** It composes a tool we already trust (single-number popcount) over a range. There's no insight required — it's a loop wrapped around a loop — which is exactly why it's the right thing to state first before optimising.

**Why it's O(n log n) and not O(n).** Each number takes time proportional to its number of set bits, which is at most `log i + 1`. Adding that up over `0..n` gives roughly `n log n` total operations. The follow-up explicitly asks you to remove that `log` factor, which is the cue to look for shared structure between consecutive numbers.

**Why we don't ship it.** It's correct and passes, but it throws away an obvious relationship: the bit count of `i` is almost the bit count of a smaller number we *just computed*. Recomputing from scratch each time is the waste the DP eliminates.
approaches.insight: Doing independent work per number is the classic 'no memoisation' smell. The moment you notice consecutive numbers share most of their bits, you should suspect a recurrence — that's the jump to the DP.

dryRun.intro: Popcount each number from scratch with Kernighan. (cnt = clears until 0.)

Independent result for each number — no reuse.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop runs once for i = 0; inner while never executes → ans = [0].

pitfalls: Mutating i directly instead of a copy — you'd lose the loop index.
Calling a builtin popcount and claiming O(n) — true with hardware popcount, but it dodges the follow-up's intent to show a recurrence.
Off-by-one on the array size — it must be n + 1, not n.

approaches.name: DP — Reuse the Right-Shifted Result (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer the follow-up wants. Say 'bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1): chop the last bit, look up the smaller number, add the bit back'.
hints: How does the binary form of i relate to the binary form of i / 2 (i.e. i >> 1)?
i >> 1 is i with its lowest bit removed. So i has all the set bits of i >> 1, plus possibly the one bit you removed.
That removed bit is exactly i & 1. So dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), and i >> 1 < i means it's already computed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each index does O(1) work — one array lookup, one shift, one AND, one add. Across n + 1 indices that's O(n) time; the only storage is the required output array, so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Fill the answer array left to right. For each `i`, look up the already-computed count for `i >> 1` and add the lowest bit `i & 1`.

**Why `i >> 1` is the subproblem.** Right-shifting by one deletes the lowest bit of `i` — it's `i` with its last binary digit chopped off. Crucially `i >> 1 < i`, so by the time we reach `i` we have *already filled* `dp[i >> 1]`. The number `i` therefore inherits every set bit of `i >> 1`.

**Why we add `i & 1`.** The only bit `i >> 1` doesn't account for is the one we chopped off — the lowest bit of `i`. That bit is `1` when `i` is odd and `0` when even, which is exactly `i & 1`. So the full count is `bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1)`. Concretely, `6 = 110` shifts to `3 = 11` (two set bits) and `6 & 1 = 0`, giving `2`; `7 = 111` shifts to the same `3 = 11` but `7 & 1 = 1`, giving `3`.

**Why the base case is `dp[0] = 0`.** Zero has no set bits, and every recurrence eventually bottoms out at it (repeated halving reaches `0`). Initialising the array to zeros gives this for free, so the loop can start at `i = 1`.

**An equivalent recurrence worth naming.** `dp[i] = dp[i & (i - 1)] + 1`: `i & (i - 1)` clears the lowest *set* bit, producing a smaller solved number, and we add `1` for the bit we cleared. Either recurrence is O(1) per element — mention both to show range.
approaches.insight: The whole speedup comes from noticing that binary numbers nest: every number is a smaller number with one extra bit on the end. Once you see bit count as 'count of the prefix + the last bit', the O(n) DP writes itself. This 'derive the big case from a structurally smaller, already-solved case' move is the essence of DP.

dryRun.intro: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Each lookup hits an index we already filled.

java.explanation: Initialised to all zeros — gives dp[0] = 0 for free, the base case.
Start at 1 since dp[0] is already correct.
Bits of i = bits of i with last digit chopped (i >> 1) plus that last bit (i & 1).

python.explanation: Zero-filled output doubles as base case dp[0] = 0.
i >> 1 < i, so the dependency is always already filled.
Reuse the smaller number's count and add the lowest bit.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop body never runs; dp stays [0]. The zero-initialised array is already the answer.
dp[8] = dp[4] + 0 = 1 (8 = 1000). Powers of two correctly resolve to a single set bit via the chain 8→4→2→1.

pitfalls: Forgetting dp[0] = 0 base case — though zero-initialising the array handles it implicitly.
Writing dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + 1 unconditionally — you must add (i & 1), which is 0 for even i.
Using the recurrence with i decreasing or referencing a not-yet-filled index — always shift toward smaller, already-computed indices.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the O(n log n) per-number popcount and not finding the linear recurrence.
Adding 1 unconditionally instead of (i & 1) — breaks on even numbers.
Sizing the output array as n instead of n + 1, dropping the last index.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Adding 1 instead of (i & 1)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only odd numbers gain a set bit over their right-shifted half. Adding 1 for even i overcounts every even index.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + 1   # wrong: even i adds a phantom bit
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1)   # add the actual lowest bit

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one array size
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The output must cover 0..n inclusive — that's n + 1 entries. Sizing it n drops the answer for i = n.

followupVariations.title: Number of 1 Bits
followupVariations.hint: The single-number building block: Brian Kernighan's n & (n - 1) popcount.

followupVariations.title: Hamming Distance
followupVariations.hint: Popcount of a ^ b. Same counting machinery on the XOR of two numbers.

followupVariations.title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero
followupVariations.hint: Halve if even, subtract 1 if odd — steps = bits + (highest bit position). Same shift/odd structure.

followupVariations.title: Total Hamming Distance
followupVariations.hint: Sum pairwise bit differences column by column — count set bits per position across all numbers.

patternNote: Bit DP / offline popcount. Recognise it when you need set-bit counts for a whole range and a larger number's answer can be built from a structurally smaller one (i >> 1 or i & (i - 1)). It's the bit-manipulation face of overlapping-subproblem DP.
